Contractor cost is a second signal, and it needs careful attribution. The 2015 Defense Business Board study, as summarized by Taxpayers for Common Sense, reported average annual costs per full-time contract worker in back-office functions of just over 189,000 dollars in the Army and just under 171,000 dollars in the Navy; these are averages for service-contract labor in those functions and are not a like-for-like comparison with civilian pay. The Project on Government Oversight’s 2011 study compared contractor billing rates with federal employee compensation across 35 occupational classifications and found federal employees cheaper in 33 of the 35, with the government paying contractors an average of 1.83 times as much; the comparison uses billing rates rather than full cost, and its scope is the occupations it sampled. GAO, in its 2018 review of the Department’s own civilian-versus-contractor cost comparisons (GAO-18-399), assessed the Department’s methodology and found that it excluded some costs; GAO did not conclude that contractors are generally more expensive, and this paper does not attribute that conclusion to it. What the sources together support is narrower: contract labor for back-office work is expensive, its full cost is not consistently measured, and congressional civilian personnel ceilings create an incentive to substitute contractors for civilians regardless of cost, a structural distortion rather than a management choice.

Decision Velocity focuses on reported decision delays. Structural Clarity examines responsibilities and authority; Operational Systems examines unnecessary process work; Institutional Performance examines reliable delivery and response to change.

Apply the idea

Examine one delayed decision.

What this affects

When decisions cannot move cleanly

When a decision stalls, can the people involved identify who owns it, why each approval is needed, and when to escalate? Institutions rarely stall because leaders hesitate. They stall because authority is unclear, approvals are layered, and signal travels through too many hands before action is possible.

Questions to ask

Where velocity breaks down

  • Who has authority to make this decision?
  • Which approvals address a specific risk?
  • Who resolves an exception or disagreement?
  • Where did the decision wait, and for how long?
  • Authority that is unclear or quietly contested
  • Approval layers heavier than the real risk warrants
  • Escalation routes that are muddy or undefined
  • Opportunities decaying while they sit in internal queues

    • Monderman view

    Velocity is coherence, not haste: the capacity to convert information into sound action at the pace the environment requires, without avoidable drag.

    What changes when it is designed for

    Decisions that move.

    Velocity is not a matter of pushing harder. It follows from clear ownership, proportionate control, and pathways designed for flow, so sound decisions reach action without avoidable drag.

What this affects

When complexity outpaces structure

Follow a recent request from start to finish. Record who handled it, which approvals it needed, and where responsibility became unclear. Inherited layers do not just slow work. They lengthen decision routes, blur accountability, and delay the conversion of strategy into action.

Questions to ask

Where the drag shows up

  • Who owns the outcome across departments?
  • Which reviews protect against a specific risk?
  • Where do people repeat work or request the same information?
  • Who can resolve a disagreement between functions?
  • Decision routes that lengthen as approvals accumulate
  • Accountability that becomes harder to trace
  • Coordination and alignment absorbing senior time
  • Governance mechanisms heavier than the environment requires

    • Monderman view

    Complexity is not the problem. The problem is inheriting more of it than your structures can absorb, interpret, and convert into effective action.

    What changes when it is governed

    A more navigable institution.

How Monderman protects access to your information, processes Diagnostic results and uses outside services. This page explains the controls operating today, what Monderman stores, which providers process data, and which certifications Monderman does not claim.

ACCESS

Access follows your role and assignment

Monderman Workspace is available by invitation. Direct Diagnostics require a signed-in member with active Workspace access. New organizations need a valid invitation to activate their evaluation. Directed campaign links authorize only the assigned Diagnostic and do not make the recipient a Workspace member.

Supabase Auth manages member sessions. Protected Workspace pages redirect signed-out users to sign in. The database or API then checks what the signed-in user is allowed to do; access does not depend on hiding buttons in the browser.

Monderman uses database row-level security and server-side authorization to restrict Workspace data access. Database policies and permissions limit users to the operations their role allows. Tables reserved for server use can have row-level security enabled with no customer policies, so browser roles cannot read or write those rows.

Workspace administrators can change the Workspace name and review status through the customer interface. Plan, usage, billing and stored Diagnostic result fields remain server-managed, with browser write permissions restricted at the database level.

Public configuration is not a secret. Browser code includes the Supabase project URL, public publishable key and public bot-verification site key. Customer database access also requires the signed-in user's session. Privileged database, payment, AI and email credentials stay on the server and are not shipped to the browser.

INVITATION-ONLY ACCESS

Current security posture

Monderman Workspace is available by invitation. This page describes controls that are operating today and avoids claiming certifications or controls that Monderman has not completed.

Browser support. Controlled release checks currently cover current Chrome/Chromium and automated WebKit rendering for public pages, generated reports, HTML and JSON downloads, responsive layouts, and opening reports for printing or PDF export. Native Safari and browser-managed print dialogs remain best-effort until dedicated native testing is complete.

DATA PROCESSING

How answers become a saved result

The public site is served as static pages. Diagnostics call a single API service on Render. Monderman's server builds the scoring input, applies versioned scoring logic and saves the result in Supabase Postgres. The browser does not set the saved score, and directed assignments use the same server process.

Optional written observations are stored and displayed separately and do not change the structured score. They are sent for AI interpretation only when that separate feature is enabled and the participant has recorded the required permission for those saved observations; the report states when they were not incorporated.

Encrypted in transit. Browser traffic to the Monderman site, API and core hosted services uses HTTPS/TLS. Payment details are entered on Stripe-hosted payment systems rather than into Monderman's own application.

The provider inventory explains what information each outside service receives and links to its security documentation. It covers Supabase, Render, Anthropic, Resend, Stripe, Cloudflare, Google, GitHub and the browser-library delivery services.

ADMINISTRATIVE DEVICES

Administrative device protection

Monderman uses CrowdStrike Falcon Go to protect the administrative devices used to operate the business. This protection applies to those devices. The website, application servers and databases are hosted separately and are not covered by this device subscription.

AI-ASSISTED REPORTS

Interpretation within Monderman's rules

AI-assisted interpretation is currently enabled for eligible Diagnostic and Synthesis reports, including evaluation reports. Optional written observations are used only when the participant has explicitly allowed the applicable processing. Earlier observations are not automatically made eligible. A saved report can show measured results before interpretation is ready; its status identifies whether interpretation is available. Restoring this service does not automatically regenerate or replace older saved reports.

What the engine determines. Monderman's diagnostic engine produces the scores, classifications, evidence limits and available action options. Anthropic's AI supports research and writes the explanation from authorized evidence within those rules. The interpretation does not change the saved score. Automated checks and a separate AI review screen the interpretation before release; they do not establish scientific validity or guarantee an outcome. Review the report before acting.

Evidence sent for a report. Selected structured answers, computed results and context are sent to Anthropic's commercial API. Synthesis of your own saved runs can include selected original structured answers and their exact questions, with each run's Diagnostic, perspective, run length and questionnaire version.

Campaign evidence. Campaign Synthesis can include descriptive answer distributions for each exact question and context, not named participants' individual answer records. Small or insufficiently supported groups are withheld. A bounded selection of permitted participant observations can also be included, with new per-run permission under the September 12 notice; an earlier permission does not authorize this expanded use.

Before drafting. The same permitted evidence and proposed report text may be sent for request-size checks before drafting or review, even if no interpretation is generated. Monderman does not send Stripe card details or Monderman service credentials with Diagnostic interpretation requests.

Research and training boundaries. Monderman does not use Customer responses, observations, reports, chat messages or organization history for model training, fine-tuning, provider feedback, shared benchmarks or cross-customer research, including in aggregated or de-identified form. Saved results remain available to authorized users within their own organization. External practice guidance comes from reviewed public or properly licensed sources.

A separate public-research process uses only predefined sector and Diagnostic categories, not customer answers, organization names or Workspace history. Reports show the research date or disclose that no newly checked research is included. Anthropic states that commercial-product inputs and outputs are not used to train its models by default unless the customer explicitly opts in or submits qualifying feedback.

ARCHITECTURE

How a Diagnostic moves from browser to saved result

The Monderman site is served as static pages over HTTPS. Direct Diagnostics require a signed-in member with active Workspace access. New organizations need a valid invitation to activate their evaluation. Directed campaign assignment links can be completed without the recipient becoming a Workspace member.

Diagnostics call a single API service on Render. Monderman calculates and saves scores using versioned application code and Supabase Postgres. When AI-assisted reporting is enabled, the server sends selected report evidence to Anthropic's commercial API for a separate written interpretation. The interpretation does not change the saved score. Service-role database credentials, Stripe secret keys, Anthropic credentials and email-provider credentials stay server-side and are not shipped to the browser.

Core outside services currently include Supabase for database and authentication, Render for the API, Anthropic for AI-assisted report interpretation when enabled, Resend for email delivery, Stripe for billing, Cloudflare for bot verification, GitHub for the static site repository and hosting workflow, and public content-delivery networks for versioned browser libraries.

CHAT

Product guidance, not access to your records

The public assistant and Hans use Anthropic for conversational product guidance, separately from report interpretation. Their requests contain a limited recent conversation, approved public product information and, for Hans, the current page and server-checked plan and role. They do not have access to source code, scoring formulas, question banks, participant records or saved report contents. Hans requires verified sign-in and eligible membership in the selected organization. Do not paste report contents, personal information, credentials or confidential, classified or controlled information into either chat.

Chat requests and replies are screened for prohibited requests, unsupported claims and unsafe links. These checks reduce risk but do not guarantee every reply is correct or every attack will be detected. The assistants cannot change a score, send a campaign, modify records or buy a subscription.

Monderman's chat application does not store transcripts in its database or intentionally log message contents; limited usage metadata supports spending controls. AI-backed API endpoints also apply request-size and rate limits to reduce automated abuse and unexpected model spend. Chat content is subject to the same no-training policy and standard provider-retention exceptions described on this page and in the Privacy Notice.

The central contrast Sentiment measurement shows where people experience strain. Systems Measurement examines the organizational systems beneath that experience.

Culture can affect performance, and operating conditions can shape culture. Use sentiment measurement to locate reported strain, then examine ownership, decisions, handoffs, and process load to understand what may be producing it.

Sentiment reports experience. Systems Measurement examines organizational mechanisms. The distinction is not a verdict on either category. It is a boundary between two kinds of evidence.

Culture can affect performance, and operating conditions can shape culture. The defensible point is narrower: a culture or sentiment score does not, by itself, identify the organizational mechanisms producing the condition.

Organizations can continue to use sentiment measurement to locate reported strain. Systems Measurement adds a distinct question: what mechanisms are people working within, and where does that system show strain?

Monderman builds organizational diagnostics that collect structured responses about ownership, decisions, administrative burden, and institutional performance. Its versioned scoring system is separate from the AI explanation of completed results.

Two kinds of evidence

Reported experienceEngagement, morale, confidence, and other self-reported signals.
Operating mechanismsOwnership, authority, handoffs, routing, process load, and performance discipline.

Sentiment measurement

  • Asks how people experience their work.
  • Locates where engagement, morale, or confidence is low.
  • Tracks changes in self-reported scores.

Systems Measurement

  • Examines the organizational mechanisms people work within.
  • Locates where ownership, authority, handoffs, routing, or process load show strain.
  • Establishes a baseline for matched remeasurement.

A low sentiment score can show where to look, but it does not identify which operating condition needs attention.

That boundary matters when a score becomes a management question. A low score can show where reported experience warrants attention. It cannot identify whether the condition is linked to unclear ownership, slow approvals, unstable handoffs, excess process load, or another operating mechanism.

The two forms of measurement answer different questions. One records how work is experienced. The other examines the structures through which work moves. Keeping the two forms of evidence distinct prevents a reported symptom from being mistaken for an explanation of the system beneath it.

How Monderman applies the distinction

Examine a defined operating scope alongside reported experience.

Monderman’s four Diagnostics collect structured responses about related parts of organizational work. Structural Clarity addresses ownership, authority, and handoffs. Decision Velocity addresses approvals, escalation, and routing. Operational Systems addresses process burden. Institutional Performance addresses the broader operating system.

Each result describes the completed responses within a defined run scope. It is not an external observation or an organization-wide finding.

Depth Synthesis summarizes eligible runs from one Diagnostic. Cross-Lens Synthesis compares eligible results from different Diagnostics and publishes a Composite Score only when the selected evidence meets the platform’s coherence rules.

The studies cited here did not test or validate Monderman’s instruments. They support examining management practices and organizational mechanisms as a distinct layer of organizational evidence.

Apply the idea

Compare the process with its original purpose.

What this affects

When complexity outpaces structure

Choose a recurring process that has become harder to complete. Compare how it works now with the problem it was designed to solve. Inherited layers do not just slow work. They lengthen decision routes, blur accountability, and delay the conversion of strategy into action.

Questions to ask

Where the drag shows up

  • What has changed since this process was designed?
  • Which temporary workarounds became permanent?
  • Which approvals still address a current need?
  • Who is responsible for reviewing the whole process?
  • Decision routes that lengthen as approvals accumulate
  • Accountability that becomes harder to trace
  • Coordination and alignment absorbing senior time
  • Governance mechanisms heavier than the environment requires

    • Monderman view

    Complexity is not the problem. The problem is inheriting more of it than your structures can absorb, interpret, and convert into effective action.

    What changes when it is governed

    A more navigable institution.

    The four Monderman diagnostics measure how your structure is actually performing, so complexity can be governed rather than absorbed. Start where the drag is greatest.

Different perspectives

Keep differences in experience visible.

People doing, managing and overseeing the same work may describe different conditions. Those differences can identify questions worth investigating. Monderman keeps participant perspectives distinct rather than hiding them in one average.

What Monderman believes

Four commitments define the work.

Commitment 01

How work moves can change over time.

Growth, reorganizations, and new controls can change approvals, ownership, handoffs, and recurring administrative work.

Commitment 02

A repeatable baseline is more useful than a one-time impression.

A later run with matching scope and settings makes differences in submitted answers and scores visible. It does not prove what caused them.

Commitment 03

Different perspectives should remain distinct.

Divergence between the people doing, managing, and governing the work can be evidence, not noise to average away.

Commitment 04

The goal is not to remove every rule or review.

Some administration protects the organization. The task is to examine which controls still serve a clear purpose and which deserve further review.
